title: Training a Transformer Model
blurb: Tests self-attention and its query, key and value vectors, the square-root scaling, multi-head attention and positional encoding, the transformer block and its three families, why transformers scale and where attention's quadratic cost bites, and the 12·L·d² parameter estimate.

ideas.title: The block and the three architecture families

refLinks.label: §29.2.3 The Transformer Block and Architecture Variants

questions.prompt: In self-attention, what role does the Key vector play?
options: It is what a token contributes to the output once it is attended to.
It says what a token is looking for in other tokens.
It stores the token's position in the sequence.
It says what a token contains. Other tokens' queries are compared against it.
questions.explanation: Query is "what am I looking for?", Key is "what do I contain?", and Value is "what should I contribute?". Scores come from Q·K, and outputs are weighted sums of V. Position comes from positional encoding.

questions.prompt: Why are attention scores divided by √d_k?
options: Large dot products push softmax toward one-hot, which kills gradients.
It normalises the output so that each row of attention weights sums to exactly 1.
It makes attention order-aware.
It reduces the memory needed to store the scores.
questions.explanation: Dot products grow with d_k. Without scaling, softmax saturates near one-hot and gradients vanish. Softmax itself makes rows sum to 1. The scale saves no memory and adds no order information.

questions.prompt: A query and a key have a dot product of 16 and d_k = 64. What is the scaled score before softmax?
questions.explanation: √64 = 8, so the scaled score is 16 / 8 = 2.

questions.prompt: A token has scaled scores of 2 and 0 against two tokens. What attention weight goes to the first token after softmax? Give three decimal places.
questions.explanation: softmax gives e² / (e² + e⁰) = 7.389 / 8.389 = 0.881. The second token gets 0.119.

questions.prompt: In Listing 29.1, what does masked_fill(mask == 0, float('-inf')) do before the softmax?
options: It sets masked positions to weight 1, so they dominate.
It gives masked positions zero weight, since e^-∞ = 0 after softmax.
It sets the masked scores to the row average.
It removes the masked positions from the value matrix before the multiply.
questions.explanation: A score of −∞ becomes exactly 0 after softmax, so those positions get no attention. That is how causal masking stops a decoder token from seeing later tokens. V keeps its shape. Only the weights change.

questions.prompt: Why does a transformer need positional encoding?
options: Attention alone ignores order, so "the cat sat" and "sat the cat" look the same.
Without it, attention scores can't be computed, because every key needs a position index.
It replaces the token embeddings in later layers.
It reduces attention's quadratic cost.
questions.explanation: Attention compares every token with every other, ignoring order. Positional encoding adds order information to each embedding. It doesn't change the cost and is added to embeddings, not substituted.

questions.prompt: What is the point of running several attention heads in parallel?
options: Each head can learn a different relationship, and their outputs are combined.
The heads vote, and the majority answer is used.
Each head handles a different slice of the sequence, so very long inputs still fit.
Extra heads add randomness, which acts like dropout.
questions.explanation: MultiHead concatenates head_1 to head_h and projects with W_o. Each head has its own Q/K/V projections, free to specialise. Heads see the whole sequence, and they are combined, not voted.

questions.prompt: How do the original transformer and most modern variants such as BERT and GPT differ on positional encoding?
options: The original used a fixed sinusoidal pattern. Most modern variants learn their position embeddings.
The original had none. Modern variants added it.
The original learned position embeddings. Most modern variants use a fixed sinusoidal pattern.
Both use the same sinusoidal pattern.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the original paper used fixed sinusoids (Listing 29.2), while BERT and GPT use learned position embeddings.

questions.prompt: Which family is the architecture behind modern chat models?
options: Encoder-only, with bidirectional context
Decoder-only, with causal masking
Encoder-decoder, as in T5
Recurrent networks such as LSTMs
questions.explanation: GPT, Llama and Claude are decoder-only. Encoder-only models like BERT can't generate text. Encoder-decoder models such as T5 suit translation and summarisation.

refLinks.label: §29.2.3 The Transformer Block and Architecture Variants

questions.prompt: What does the residual connection x + sublayer(x) do for a deep transformer stack?
options: It gives gradients a shortcut, which makes deep stacks trainable.
It lets each block see future tokens.
It replaces layer normalisation.
It halves the parameter count of each block by sharing weights across layers.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the residual path is what makes very deep stacks trainable at all. It adds no parameters, it sits alongside layer normalisation, and it has nothing to do with masking.

refLinks.label: §29.2.3 The Transformer Block and Architecture Variants

questions.prompt: A team needs named-entity tagging on documents and never needs to generate text. Which family fits best?
options: Encoder-only, since it reads context on both sides of each token
Decoder-only, because it is the most widely used family for every task
None. Transformers can't do NER.
Encoder-decoder, because NER is a translation task
questions.explanation: Encoder-only models see context on both sides of each token, which suits tagging. A decoder's causal mask hides the right-hand context. NER is not a sequence-to-sequence generation task.

questions.prompt: Why do transformers train so much faster than LSTMs on long sequences?
options: Transformers skip the backward pass.
QKᵀ covers all positions in one matrix multiply. An LSTM steps token by token.
Transformers have far fewer parameters than LSTMs, so each training step is cheaper.
LSTMs can't run on GPUs.
questions.explanation: An LSTM on 1,000 tokens takes 1,000 sequential steps. A transformer processes all 1,000 in parallel. That parallelism is why scaling laws hold: the compute can be used efficiently.

questions.prompt: Attention cost is O(n²) in sequence length. If the context grows from 4,000 to 8,000 tokens, by what factor does the attention computation grow?
questions.explanation: Every token attends to every other, so cost scales with n². Doubling n gives 2² = 4 times the work.

questions.prompt: Where does the chapter say transformers lose? Select all that apply.
options: Resource-constrained inference, where a BERT-scale model is 100 to 400 MB
Tabular data, where XGBoost still typically dominates
Very small datasets, where classical models generalise better
Tasks with long-range dependencies in text
questions.explanation: The trade-offs section lists tabular data, very small datasets and constrained inference. Long-range dependencies in text are where transformers win.

questions.prompt: In N ≈ 12 · n_layers · d_model², where does the 12 come from?
options: Four d×d attention matrices plus two d×4d feed-forward matrices: 4 + 8 = 12.
Three matrices (Q, K, V) times four bytes per parameter.
Twelve attention heads per layer, each holding its own d² parameters for Q, K and V.
Twelve layers in a standard model.
questions.explanation: W_q, W_k, W_v and W_o are 4d², and the feed-forward block adds d×4d and 4d×d, which is 8d². Head count doesn't change the total, since heads split d_model between them. Bytes per parameter is a memory figure.

questions.prompt: Estimate the non-embedding parameters of a model with 24 layers and d_model = 1024, using 12 · n_layers · d_model². Give the answer in millions, to the nearest million.
GPT-2 small has 12 layers, d_model = 768 and a 50,257-token vocabulary. Using the formula plus the embedding matrix (vocab × d_model), what is the estimate, in millions to one decimal place?
For GPT-2 small, the embedding matrix is about 31% of the estimate. What does that say about when the embedding term matters?
options: It never matters, since the formula is under 1% off without it.
It matters only for encoder-only models like DistilBERT.
It matters for large models only, since vocabularies grow along with model size.
It matters for small models. At scale, 12·L·d² grows faster and dwarfs it.
questions.explanation: 38.6M of 123.5M is about 31%. The layer term grows with L·d², the embedding only with d, so it shrinks as a share at scale. The chapter calls it non-trivial for small models. The under-1% error includes the embedding term, and it matters for GPT-2 (decoder-only) too.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, what happens to attention from "it" to "animal" versus "street" across DistilBERT's layers?
options: The word "it" attends more to "street" in every layer.
The two are equal in every layer, so the model never resolves "it" at all.
It is strongest in layer 0 and fades in later layers.
It peaks in layer 4, at nearly six times the weight on "street".
questions.explanation: Layer 4 averages 0.1688 to "animal" against 0.0289 to "street", a ratio of about 5.8. Layer 0 slightly favours "street" (0.0462 against 0.0364), so the resolution builds up in middle layers.

questions.prompt: DistilBERT was never trained on coreference. Where does the "it" → "animal" behaviour come from?
options: From the positional encoding, which links nearby pronouns and nouns.
From the tokenizer, which tags pronouns with their referents.
It emerged from masked-language-model pretraining alone.
From a coreference head added during fine-tuning.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the behaviour emerged from masked-language-model pretraining with no explicit coreference signal. "it" and "animal" are not even adjacent, and the tokenizer doesn't tag referents.

questions.prompt: Layer 4, head 1 gives "animal" weight 0.513 and "street" 0.029. A colleague says this proves the model "understands" coreference everywhere. What is a fair reading?
options: It proves the model resolves every pronoun correctly.
It proves nothing, since attention weights are random.
It is real evidence from one head on one sentence. A general claim needs more tests.
It shows head 1 is the only head that matters, and the others could be removed.
questions.explanation: The chapter shows a specific layer and head encoding the resolution, found by looking. That is one measured case. Generalising needs a wider test. Attention weights are learned, not random, and other heads may do other jobs.

bookExercises.prompt: Write the attention score formula $\text{score}(i,j)$ and explain in one sentence what the $\sqrt{d_k}$ term prevents.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `score(i, j) = softmax(Qᵢ · Kⱼ / √d_k)`. The √d_k term prevents the dot products `Qᵢ · Kⱼ` from growing large as `d_k` increases, which would otherwise push softmax into a near-one-hot regime with vanishing gradients everywhere except the single largest score.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the three architecture families (encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder), give one example model for each, and state which family cannot generate text.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Encoder-only (e.g. BERT), decoder-only (e.g. GPT-2), encoder-decoder (e.g. T5). Encoder-only models cannot generate text. They see full bidirectional context, which is well-suited to classification/understanding tasks but incompatible with left-to-right generation.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 29.5's measured results, explain what "layer 4 attends to 'animal' with weight 0.1688 versus 0.0289 to 'street', averaged across heads" tells you about where in the network coreference resolution is happening, and why checking multiple layers (not just the last one) was necessary to find this.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Layer 4 attending to "animal" with weight 0.1688 versus 0.0289 to "street" (averaged across all 12 heads) indicates that coreference-relevant information has been built up by the middle-to-later layers of the network. Earlier layers (0–1) show much weaker and less consistent differentiation (0.0364 vs 0.0462 at layer 0, actually favoring "street" slightly). Checking multiple layers was necessary because attention patterns are not uniform across depth. A single layer chosen arbitrarily (especially an early one) could have shown the opposite or a null result, giving a misleading impression that the model doesn't encode this resolution at all.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 29.6's table, compute the formula estimate for a model with $n_{\text{layers}}=32$, $d_{\text{model}}=4096$, vocab=32,000, and state whether this is consistent with the chapter calling this "roughly a 7B model."
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `12 × 32 × 4096² = 12 × 32 × 16,777,216 = 6,442,450,944 ≈ 6.44B`. Adding vocab×d_model with vocab=32,000: `32,000 × 4096 = 131,072,000 ≈ 0.13B`, giving a total of roughly 6.57B parameters. That's consistent with the chapter's claim that this configuration lands "in the right ballpark for a 7B model" once minor terms are included.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague claims "DistilBERT was explicitly trained to resolve pronoun coreference, that's why 'it' attends to 'animal'." Using this chapter's Worked Example, correct this claim in two or three sentences.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "DistilBERT was pretrained purely with a masked-language-modelling objective, predicting randomly masked tokens from context, with no coreference-specific labels or task anywhere in its training. The attention pattern favoring 'animal' over 'street' for 'it' emerged as a side effect of learning to predict masked words well, which requires implicitly tracking what pronouns refer to. It's a learned regularity, not an explicitly trained capability."

bookExercises.prompt: The parameter-count formula in Exposition ignores the embedding matrix. Using Listing 29.6's table, compute how many percentage points of error the GPT-2 estimate would have WITHOUT adding the embedding term (formula-only was 84,934,656 against an actual of 124,439,808), and explain why the embedding term matters more for GPT-2 than it would for a much larger model.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Formula-only (no embedding term) gives 84,934,656 against an actual 124,439,808, an error of `(84,934,656 - 124,439,808) / 124,439,808 ≈ -31.7%`, a far larger error than the -0.73% achieved once the embedding term is added. The embedding term matters more for GPT-2 small specifically because its vocabulary (50,257 tokens) is large relative to its total parameter count (124M). The embedding matrix alone (50,257 × 768 ≈ 38.6M) is nearly a third of the whole model. A much larger model (e.g. a 70B-parameter model) has a similarly-sized vocabulary but a vastly larger `12·L·d²` term, so the same embedding matrix becomes a negligible fraction of the total, and the formula-only estimate would be accurate even without adding it.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about why attention has $O(n^2)$ complexity in sequence length. Identify one specific technique mentioned in this chapter (sliding-window attention or linear attention) that reduces this, and explain at a high level what it gives up to do so.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Sliding-window attention restricts each token to attending only within a fixed-size local window (e.g. the nearest 512 tokens) rather than the entire sequence, reducing complexity from O(n²) to O(n·w) where w is the window size. What it gives up: a token far outside the window has no direct attention path to it in a single layer. Long-range dependencies must instead propagate indirectly across multiple stacked layers (each layer's window effectively "reaches" a bit further than the last), which is a weaker and less direct mechanism than the original architecture's ability for any token to attend to any other token in one step.
